questions.0.question.source: The Riverstone drawing shows a river. The diary says traders came by boat. What do these two clues suggest together?
questions.0.question.back: The drawing of Riverstone market has a river. The diary says traders came by boat. Looking at these two clues together, what do they point to?
questions.0.question.note: "diary" as บันทึกประจำวัน and "traders" as พ่อค้าแม่ค้า (gender-neutral pair). Check these match the words chosen in Lesson 1. Second pass: Checked: Lesson 1 uses บันทึกประจำวัน and พ่อค้าแม่ค้า. Flag removed.

questions.1.stimulus.title.source: A made-up source: a poster from the town of Norrin, about 40 years ago
questions.1.stimulus.title.back: Fictional source: a poster from the town of Norrin, about 40 years ago

questions.1.stimulus.items.1.source: On Saturday, in the town hall.
questions.1.stimulus.items.1.note: "town hall" as หอประชุมเมือง (ศาลากลาง would suggest a provincial government office). Check.

questions.1.question.source: A historian finds this poster. Which question needs a different source to answer?
questions.1.question.back: A historian finds this poster. Which question needs another source to answer?

questions.1.options.0.text.back: Where was the book fair held?

questions.1.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The poster says the fair was in the town hall. So the poster can answer this. Look back at Lesson 1.
questions.1.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. The poster says it was at the town hall, so the poster answers this question. Go back to Lesson 1.

questions.1.options.1.text.source: What time did story time start?
questions.1.options.1.text.back: What time did the storytelling start?

questions.1.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The poster says story time was at 10:00. So the poster can answer this. Look back at Lesson 1.
questions.1.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. The poster says storytelling was at 10:00, so the poster answers this question. Go back to Lesson 1.

questions.1.options.2.text.source: How many people came to it?
questions.1.options.2.text.back: How many people came to the fair?

questions.1.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. The poster does not say how many people came. A historian would need another source, like a diary or a photo.
questions.1.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. The poster doesn't say how many people came. The historian needs another source, such as a diary or a photo.

questions.2.stimulus.title.source: A made-up object: a wooden spoon from the village of Tavi
questions.2.stimulus.title.back: Fictional object: a wooden spoon from the village of Tavi

questions.2.stimulus.items.1.source: One end is dark and burned.
questions.2.stimulus.items.1.back: One end is black and burnt

questions.2.stimulus.items.2.source: There is a small crack in the handle.
questions.2.stimulus.items.2.back: There is a small crack on the handle

questions.2.stimulus.items.3.source: A star is cut into the handle.
questions.2.stimulus.items.3.back: A star is carved on the handle

questions.2.question.source: Which sentence about the spoon is an inference?
questions.2.question.back: Which sentence about the spoon is an inference?

questions.2.options.0.text.source: The handle has a star cut into it.
questions.2.options.0.text.back: A star is carved on the handle

questions.2.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. You can see the star on the handle, so this is an observation. Look back at Lesson 2.
questions.2.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. You can see the star on the handle, so this sentence is an observation. Go back to Lesson 2.

questions.2.options.1.text.source: It may have been used near a fire.
questions.2.options.1.text.back: This spoon may have been used near a fire

questions.2.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Nobody can see the fire now. You build this idea from a clue, the burned end. That makes it an inference.
questions.2.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. No one can see that fire now. You thought of this from a clue, the burnt end, so this sentence is an inference.

questions.2.options.2.text.source: There is a small crack in the handle.
questions.2.options.2.text.back: There is a small crack on the handle

questions.2.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. You can see the crack for yourself, so this is an observation. Look back at Lesson 2.
questions.2.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. You can see the crack yourself, so this sentence is an observation. Go back to Lesson 2.

questions.3.question.source: What can a close view of the past show that a wide view may hide?
questions.3.question.back: What can a close-up view show about the past that a wide view might hide?
questions.3.question.note: "close view" / "wide view" as มุมมองระยะใกล้ / มุมมองแบบกว้าง. These are not in KEY_TERMS; make them match whatever Lesson 3 uses. Second pass: "close view" now มุมมองแบบใกล้, the words Lesson 3 uses (beside มุมมองแบบกว้าง); it said มุมมองระยะใกล้. Second pass: Flag removed: it now matches Lesson 3.

questions.3.options.0.text.source: How a town grew over 100 years
questions.3.options.0.text.back: How a town grew over 100 years

questions.3.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Growth over 100 years is a pattern. A wide view is good at showing patterns. Look back at Lesson 3.
questions.3.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. Growth over 100 years is a pattern. A wide view helps you see patterns well. Go back to Lesson 3.

questions.3.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. A close view, like one diary, shows one person's choices and feelings. A wide view can hide people.
questions.3.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. A close-up view, such as one diary, shows one person's decisions and feelings. A wide view may hide people.
questions.3.options.1.feedback.note: Second pass: มุมมองแบบใกล้, as in Lesson 3.

questions.3.options.2.text.source: How a river moved over a long time
questions.3.options.2.text.back: How a river changed its course over a long time

questions.3.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. A river that moves over hundreds of years is a pattern. A wide view shows this best. Look back at Lesson 3.
questions.3.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. A river changing course over hundreds of years is a pattern. A wide view shows this best. Go back to Lesson 3.

questions.4.question.source: Each kind of account answers its own kind of question. Which of these would a historian ask about an origin account?

questions.4.options.0.text.source: How did the sun and the planets form?
questions.4.options.0.text.back: How did the sun and planets form?

questions.4.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Scientists ask questions like this about nature. Historians ask who told an account, when and why. Look back at Lesson 4.
questions.4.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. Scientists ask this kind of question about nature. A historian asks who told the account, when and why. Go back to Lesson 4.

questions.4.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Faith accounts and cultural accounts often answer questions like this. Historians ask who told an account, and why. Look back at Lesson 4.
questions.4.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. Faith-based and cultural accounts often answer this kind of question. A historian asks who told the account and why. Go back to Lesson 4.

Second pass: "Faith accounts" now คำอธิบายทางความเชื่อ, Lesson 4's words; it said คำอธิบายตามความเชื่อทางศาสนา, which Lesson 4 never uses.

questions.4.options.2.text.source: Who told this account, and why?
questions.4.options.2.text.back: Who told this account, and why?

questions.4.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Historians ask who told an account, when and why. Each kind of question needs its own kind of answer.
questions.4.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. A historian asks who told the account, when and why. Each kind of question needs its own kind of answer.

questions.5.question.source: A young person learns a skill from an older person. She makes it better. Then she teaches it to her friends. What is this called?
questions.5.question.back: A young woman learns a skill from an older person. She makes the skill better, then teaches it to her friends. What is this called?

questions.5.options.0.text.note: KEY_TERMS gives การเรียนรู้ร่วมกัน for "collective learning"; in everyday Thai it can just mean "learning together", which makes the wrong options look a little less plausible than in English. Check.

questions.5.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. In collective learning, people share what they know, make it better and pass it on. This is how knowledge grows.
questions.5.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. In collective learning, people share what they know, improve it and pass it on. This is how knowledge grows.

questions.5.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Trade means you give something and get something back. Here, a skill is shared and made better. Look back at Lesson 5.
questions.5.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. Trade is giving something and getting something back. Here, a skill is shared and improved. Go back to Lesson 5.

questions.5.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Foraging means finding wild food. This example is about sharing a skill and making it better. Look back at Lesson 5.
questions.5.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. Foraging is finding food from nature. This example is about sharing a skill and improving it. Go back to Lesson 5.

questions.6.question.source: Archaeologists found these clues at early human sites. Which clue could show what people cooked?
questions.6.question.back: An archaeologist finds these clues where early humans lived. Which clue can tell what food people cooked?

questions.6.options.0.text.source: The handprints on a rock wall

questions.6.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Handprints are a kind of art. They tell us other things, not what people cooked. Look back at Lesson 5.
questions.6.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. Handprints are a kind of art; they tell us other things, not what food people cooked. Go back to Lesson 5.

questions.6.options.1.text.source: The hearth with its burned seeds

questions.6.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. A hearth is a place where people made a fire. Burned seeds in a hearth can show what people cooked.
questions.6.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. A hearth is where people made fires. Burnt seeds in a hearth can tell what food people cooked.

questions.6.options.2.text.source: Tools of the same shape, far apart
questions.6.options.2.text.back: Tools of the same shape found far apart

questions.6.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. These tools may show that people shared ideas. They do not show what people cooked. Look back at Lesson 5.
questions.6.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. These tools may show people shared ideas, but they don't tell what food people cooked. Go back to Lesson 5.

questions.7.question.source: After a good harvest, a farming village may have a surplus. What is a surplus?
questions.7.question.back: After a good harvest, a farming village may have a surplus. What is a surplus?

questions.7.options.0.text.source: More food than people need right now
questions.7.options.0.text.back: More food than people need now

questions.7.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. A surplus is food left over. People can store it, so not everyone has to farm.

questions.7.options.1.text.source: A plant that people grow for food

questions.7.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. A plant that people grow for food is a crop. A surplus is extra food or goods. Look back at Lesson 6.
questions.7.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. Plants people grow for food are crops. A surplus is food or goods left over. Go back to Lesson 6.

questions.7.options.2.text.source: Finding wild food instead of growing it
questions.7.options.2.text.back: Going to find food in the wild instead of growing it

questions.7.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. Finding food in the wild is called foraging. A surplus is more food than people need now. Go back to Lesson 6.

questions.8.question.source: Banwa is a made-up city. Many things change there over time. Which of these changes shows that some people gained more power than others?
questions.8.question.back: Banwa is a fictional town where many things changed over time. Which change shows that some people had more power than others?

questions.8.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. Spare grain helped Banwa grow, but doesn't show who had more power. Go back to Lesson 7.

questions.8.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. A shared storehouse shows people working together. It does not show who has more power. Look back at Lesson 7.
questions.8.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. A shared granary shows people worked together, but doesn't show who had more power. Go back to Lesson 7.

questions.8.options.2.text.source: Some families control more land and grain

questions.8.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. Families with more land and grain had more power. In early towns, power wasn't shared equally.

questions.9.question.source: In Babylon, King Hammurabi had rules carved on a tall stone. Everyone had to follow them. What are rules like these called?
questions.9.question.back: In Babylon, King Hammurabi had regulations carved on a tall stone. Everyone had to follow them. What are regulations like this called?
questions.9.question.note: "rules" as ข้อบังคับ so the question does not contain กฎ, which would give away the answer กฎหมาย. Royal vocabulary kept plain (สั่งให้สลัก) as KEY_TERMS asks. Second pass: kept ข้อบังคับ for that reason, although the feedback defines law with กฎ.

questions.9.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. A tax is something people give to their government, like grain or work. Look back at Lesson 7.
questions.9.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. Taxes are what people give to the government, such as grain or labour. Go back to Lesson 7.

questions.9.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. A law is a rule that everyone in a place must follow. Hammurabi had about 280 laws carved on a stone.
questions.9.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. Laws are rules everyone in a place must follow. Hammurabi had about 280 laws carved on the stone.

questions.9.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Goods are things people make or grow, like jars or cloth. Look back at Lesson 7.
questions.9.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. Goods are things people make or grow, such as jars or cloth. Go back to Lesson 7.

questions.10.question.source: Paper was first made in China. How did the idea of papermaking reach the Middle East and Europe?
questions.10.question.back: Paper was first made in China. How did knowledge of papermaking reach the Middle East and Europe?
questions.10.question.note: "the idea of papermaking" as ความรู้เรื่องการทำกระดาษ (knowledge of papermaking), which reads more naturally than ความคิด here.

questions.10.options.0.text.source: It spread along the trade routes.

questions.10.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Traders carried ideas as well as goods. Papermaking spread along the routes to other lands.
questions.10.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. Traders carried ideas, not just goods. Papermaking spread along routes to other lands.

questions.10.options.1.text.source: Each place made it at the same time.
questions.10.options.1.text.back: Every place made paper at the same time

questions.10.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Paper was first made in China. The idea reached other lands later. Look back at Lesson 8.
questions.10.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. Paper was first made in China; this knowledge reached other lands later. Go back to Lesson 8.

questions.10.options.2.text.source: One trader took it on one long trip.
questions.10.options.2.text.back: One trader took it on a single long journey

questions.10.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The idea did not travel in one trip. It moved along trade routes, from place to place. Look back at Lesson 8.
questions.10.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. The knowledge didn't arrive in a single journey; it moved slowly along trade routes, from place to place. Go back to Lesson 8.
